cards.b:
Remove tigers, and deer may boom; remove bees, and crops fall. Ecology studies how living things relate to each other and to their surroundings. It underpins climate policy, farming and conservation.

Ecologists often study food webs. When wolves were removed from Yellowstone in the 1920s, elk grew in number and grazed willow along rivers heavily. Likewise, in India, the decline of vultures in the 1990s after the veterinary drug diclofenac poisoned them led to more feral dogs and a risk of rabies, a case showing how one species' loss ripples. Ecology therefore connects organisms to water, soil, climate and people.

Organism, population (one species in one place), community (all species), ecosystem (community plus non-living environment: water, soil, light) and biosphere. The word 'ecology' was coined by Ernst Haeckel in 1866; 'ecosystem' by Arthur Tansley in 1935.

Take a pond as an example: one fish is an organism, all the fish of one species make a population, fish, plants, insects and microbes together are a community, and add the water, mud, sunlight and dissolved oxygen to get an ecosystem. The biosphere is the thin layer of Earth where life exists, from the deep sea to about the clouds. Within each ecosystem, a habitat is the place an organism lives, and its niche is its role.

Energy enters as sunlight and moves up through producers (plants), herbivores, carnivores and decomposers. Only about 10 percent of energy passes to the next level (Lindeman, 1942), the rest is lost as heat. That is why food chains are short and there are fewer tigers than deer.

Matter recycles; energy does not. Carbon cycle: CO2 taken in by photosynthesis, returned by respiration and burning. Nitrogen cycle: bacteria fix N2 into usable forms; others return it to air. Water cycle: evaporation, rain, runoff. Extra CO2 from fossil fuels is warming Earth.

Think of it as a one-way street for energy and a roundabout for matter. In the nitrogen cycle, bacteria in the root nodules of pulses such as peas and gram fix nitrogen from air, which is why farmers rotate pulses with cereals. Other bacteria turn waste into ammonia and nitrates, and denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the air. Fritz Haber's ammonia process (1909) now supplies fertiliser, though runoff can cause algal blooms in lakes. Charles Keeling's curve shows CO2 above 420 ppm.

Populations grow fast at first, then level off at the carrying capacity. Species interact by competition, predation, parasitism, mutualism (bees and flowers) and commensalism. Keystone species, like tigers, wolves and sea otters, have an outsized effect.

A growth curve is S-shaped: slow start, rapid rise as resources are abundant, and then levelling off as food, space or disease limit the population. Mutualism helps both sides: bees get nectar and flowers get pollinated. Parasitism helps one at the other's cost, as with ticks. A keystone species has an effect far beyond its numbers: sea otters keep sea urchins in check, which protects kelp forests, as Robert Paine's starfish removal experiments of the 1960s also showed. Tigers help keep the whole forest healthy by controlling herbivore numbers.

Bare rock turns to forest through ecological succession: lichens, mosses, grasses, shrubs, trees. Major biomes are tundra, taiga, temperate forest, grassland, desert, tropical rainforest and aquatic zones. Climate sets the biome.

On bare rock, hardy pioneer species such as lichens begin, making thin soil as they die and decay, which lets mosses and grasses take hold, and later shrubs and trees. The final stable community is the climax. India shows many biomes: the Thar desert, the Himalayan alpine zone, tropical rainforest in the Western Ghats and Northeast, mangroves in the Sundarbans and grasslands in the Terai. Rainfall and temperature, more than anything else, decide which biome forms in a place.

Threats: habitat loss, invasive species, pollution, over-harvest and climate change (summed up as HIPPO). Conservation is by protected areas (in situ: national parks, reserves) or off-site (ex situ: zoos, seed banks). Edward O. Wilson popularised the term biodiversity.

Biodiversity means variety at three levels: genes, species and ecosystems. India holds about 8 percent of the world's species on 2.4 percent of its land area, and four global hotspots (the Himalaya, Western Ghats, Indo-Burma and Sundaland). Project Tiger, begun in 1973, and the Wildlife Protection Act of 1972 are examples of in situ conservation. Ex situ options include botanical gardens, seed banks and captive breeding, such as for the Asiatic lion's second home. Healthy ecosystems also provide services like clean water and pollination.

Tansley (1935) and Lindeman (1942) quantified energy flow. Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) showed pesticide DDT harmed birds. Wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995 and rivers and plants changed (trophic cascade). Keeling's curve has shown CO2 rising since 1958.

Raymond Lindeman's work on a lake showed that only about 10 percent of energy passes from one level to the next, which is why food chains are short and why there are few top predators. Rachel Carson's book showed that DDT builds up through the food chain (biomagnification) and thins bird eggshells, and helped lead to the ban on DDT use in farming in the US in 1972. Reintroducing wolves at Yellowstone is a well-known but still debated example of a trophic cascade.

Fix these

  • Energy does not cycle; matter does.
  • The top predator is not the 'most important'; every link matters.
  • Climate and weather are different: climate is the long-term pattern.

Also, ecosystems can recover, but not always to what they were: some changes, such as the loss of a coral reef, are hard to reverse. 'Natural' does not mean unchanging, either. Weather is what happens today; climate is the average over at least thirty years, so one cold day does not disprove warming.

Also, a food web is not a ladder: an animal such as a bear or a human eats at several levels, so removing one species can have effects that are hard to predict. Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria are just as vital, since they return nutrients to the soil.

India has about 100 national parks and over 500 wildlife sanctuaries. Chipko (1973) and the Bishnoi tradition show community conservation. The Biological Diversity Act (2002) and Wildlife (Protection) Act (1972) give legal protection. Silent Valley (Kerala) was saved from a dam in the 1980s. Sundarbans is the world's largest mangrove delta. Madhav Gadgil's Western Ghats work shaped debates. India pledged net zero by 2070 at COP26 (2021).

• Energy flows one way; matter cycles.
  • About 10 percent passes up each level.
  • Biodiversity loss is driven mostly by habitat change.
  • Conservation: in situ and ex situ.

Think about it:

  1. Why is a vegetarian diet more energy-efficient?
  2. Why do keystone species matter more than their numbers suggest?

quiz.q: About how much energy passes up a level?
